positions.commentary: The speaker mentions that they were able to figure out that the issue with META was not Facebook or Instagram going away, as usage has been fine.
The speaker estimates that Google's enterprise value probably comes 15 to 20% from Google Cloud, but notes that applying a PE multiple approach effectively puts a $0 valuation on Google Cloud.

thesis: The episode argues that Google faces significant risks due to a lack of clear future vision and leadership capable of making decisive, risky moves, potentially requiring a founder's return to navigate a transition where search may become obsolete. Conversely, Meta is viewed as bearing substantial downside risk if it fails to successfully cannibalize its core feed for Reels or find new profitable projects beyond its current search-dependent model, with the speaker noting a shift from purely bearish to a more nuanced view regarding user retention.

claims.claim: The speaker worries Google management lacks a clear future vision to motivate the organization, risking the business's ability to monetize as well as it currently does.
claims.quote: But if they don't have a vision of the future in a way to motivate their organization to move towards that, then it is kind of unclear exactly, not only how this is going going to all unfold, but whether or not this business at the end of the day is going to be able to monetize anywhere near as well as it currently does.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that if Sundar Pichai leaves and Google falls, it would not be because of him, but implies the current leadership faces a risky position where a founder returning might be needed to make decisive risky moves.
claims.quote: Because these are the kind of decisions where, you know, if Sundar Pichai lives where, you know, if Sundar Pichai leaves tomorrow and then Google falls, let's say, one of the co-founders comes back, Google falls, Sooner Pichai will probably not be the key story in Google's, let's say, fall, all, right?

claims.claim: The speaker notes that even if Google fails to successfully transition its current predicament, they would hesitate to write the company off entirely because it is too big of a business.
claims.quote: Even if Google fails to really successfully transition this current predicament that they face, I would even still hesitate to totally write them off. Because these are too big of a business.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Google had $300 billion in revenue and $7-8 billion in other bets losses, comparing it to Meta's revenue and losses.
claims.quote: Google has a $300 billion dollar revenue and seven, eight billion dollar other bits losses versus meta has $130, $35 billion revenue.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Google spent $17 billion on losses in Reality Labs, which they view as a negative aspect of having a leader who cannot make such large spending decisions.
claims.quote: I don't think Sundar Pichai would be able to spend $17 billion losses in reality labs. right? So that's kind of a negative aspect of having all that, right?

claims.claim: The speaker recalls that in 2012, Google was trading at 12 times earnings, and over the next seven or eight years, EBIT was 10 times over, making it seem easy in hindsight.
claims.quote: Google was trading at 12 times in it. In that 2012, oh, that was easy, right? People don't realize what people are worried about in 2012. People don't realize what people are worried about in 2015, 2016, 2017, right?

claims.claim: Even if search becomes obsolete, Google could remain a trillion-dollar company and influential by 2030.
claims.quote: Imagine this, 2030. Google is a trillion dollar valuation. like 40% drawdown over the course of a decade, right? And it would still be a trillion dollar company. It would still be very influential.

claims.claim: Google could potentially be okay in a chat bot world because it can still suggest answers and put ads against them.
claims.quote: I'm actually, I think if the world does go the way of the chat bots, Google could potentially actually be okay in a scenario because you can see that as long as we get to the position where the user still has a choice, then there's the optionality for a suggestion to come in.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks the risk/reward for Meta is not worth it given the significant downside if they cannot make Reels work.
claims.quote: But the risk reward is just not worth it. If they can't make it work, there's a significant downside. This is exactly how I feel about Google, by the way.

claims.claim: The speaker doubts Meta can successfully cannibalize its feed to roll out Reels while taking hits from ATT.
claims.quote: If you didn't have an owner-operator that was able to say, I'm going to roll out reels, I'm going to cannibalize the feed, I'm going to simultaneously take the hit from ATT.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks the change Meta is attempting is bigger than what Zuckerberg did with the family of apps.
claims.quote: The change is bigger than what Zuckerberg was doing on family of apps. I think it's bigger. The change is bigger. And it's even harder because Zuckerberg had a lot of monetizable surfaces, right?

claims.quote: Even today, Reels is what, 25% of, like, or like, it's even more. Like, sorry, 40% of their time span, right? And in terms of revenue and profit, even lower.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Google's valuation is flawed because investors are willing to pay high multiples on short-term earnings despite the company losing money on its other bets and having a short-term CEO horizon.
claims.quote: my basically main conclusion for doubling down on Google was this is clearly flawed. I'm not going to pay zero a lot to own Google Cloud. I'm going to pay a lot more money than that, right?

claims.quote: The question is whether then when the economy comes back, whether meta still has the users, whether it still has the business that they used to have and whether they can keep growing over the course of the economic cycle.
